findings.requirement: List every built-in tool, MCP server, API, program, and file permission this agent type can use. Give a task-based reason for each. Enforce a role-based allowlist, and check that an unlisted tool can't be called. Don't base allow or approval decisions on hints a server gives about its own tools, such as "read-only." MCP treats those hints as untrusted unless you trust the server.

findings.title: Least-privilege access
findings.requirement: Limit credentials to named operations and resources, including tenant boundaries. Identify the acting agent separately from the original user or system whose authority it uses. Explicitly authorized, narrowly scoped user delegation is valid; copying a login session or inheriting a person's full permissions is not. Test that an allowed read works and an out-of-scope write, an admin action, and another tenant's data all fail. Limit each access token to its intended audience, so other services reject it. Remove wildcard grants.

not_covered.problem: A retrieval search or cache not filtered by the requesting tenant or user
Long-lived or static secrets that never expire or rotate
Revocation delay from cached or self-contained tokens
A sub-agent getting powers beyond its task, or a parent escalating through a peer
Memory readable across tenants or tasks

findings.title: Credential lifetime and handling
findings.requirement: Issue short-lived credentials from a trusted issuer or managed identity service. For API calls, use expiring access tokens with a specific destination audience, identifying the agent and any explicitly delegated user or system authority, rather than static API keys or personal access tokens. A secrets vault stores backing secrets; it does not itself make a static key into an expiring access token. Keep long-lived secrets out of prompts, images, and checked-in config. Where supported, bind tokens to their holder (mTLS, DPoP, or workload proof tokens). Don't use fixed API keys when short-lived or federated credentials are available. If only static keys are supported, isolate them at the enforcement layer, limit their permissions, and record the lifetime and revocation gap. Show expiry and rotation, including allowed overlap, and explain the chosen lifetime.

not_covered.problem: A credential scoped to more operations, resources, or tenants than needed
No way to cut off the agent's access without cutting off the user
Secrets showing up in tool output, responses, or normal logs
Container image not pinned by digest or signature-checked

findings.title: Independent revocation
findings.requirement: Show that an operator can cut off this agent's access without cutting off the user who launched it. The agent must not need to cooperate. Set and measure the longest time before the cutoff takes effect. Count cached tokens, self-contained tokens, and open sessions. A trusted enforcement point must block later calls within a time limit that fits the potential harm. Revoking only the refresh token is not enough. If tokens live longer than that limit, push the revocation to each service (for example, with OpenID CAEP session-revoked events) or make the tokens shorter-lived.

Sub-agents or remote workers still acting after the parent is stopped
Static API keys used where short-lived credentials are available
No way to trace a suspicious action to its team, operator, and live instance

findings.title: Destructive-action interception
findings.requirement: List the high-impact operations. These include deletes, destructive database updates, force-pushes, tearing down infrastructure, payment changes, and sending anything outside. Block them by default in the execution path. Allow one only when a reviewer or system with higher authority approves that specific action. When the action runs, authorize its operation, target, and arguments, and block it if they aren't allowed. A list of blocked words or command names is not enough. Test other tools and raw API or shell paths that could do the same thing. Treat deleting audit records, or changing how long they are kept, as high-impact too. findings.title: Minimal, isolated runtime
findings.requirement: Remove shells, downloaders, package managers, mounts, and privileges the agent doesn't need. As a container baseline, meet the Kubernetes Pod Security Standards "restricted" profile or the same controls elsewhere. That means non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, and a seccomp profile set. Where supported, also use a read-only root filesystem and user namespaces; the restricted profile doesn't require those two. For running untrusted code, use a sandbox that fits the threat, such as a microVM or a user-space kernel. Ordinary containers share the host's kernel. For managed runtimes, record the provider's isolation evidence and what you can't see. Test that host access is blocked. A blocked probe does not prove the sandbox resists every escape.

findings.title: Complete release manifest
findings.requirement: Write a release manifest: a list of everything that makes up this release. Include the container, harness, system prompt, rules files, model, built-in tools, MCP servers, permission scopes, memory and retrieval settings, identity bindings, network rules, and execution budgets. Include security-policy versions, MCP protocol and extension versions, approved tool-publication config, issuer/audience bindings, and cache/task isolation settings. Add a separate model record for every model: the main agent model, sub-agent models, and helper models such as embedding models and rerankers. For each, record the provider, model ID, exact version or checkpoint, and any adapter or fine-tune version. For training or fine-tuning you run yourself, also record the training job ID, base-model version, training code and config version, dataset version, and the digest of the output. The agent app's release number alone is not enough. Use the [model provenance fields](CHECKLIST-VERIFICATION.md#model-provenance-fields) to separate recorded versions from details a provider doesn't share. Check each model ID you request against the provider's versioning docs. Mark it as a pinned snapshot or as an alias that can change, and record which doc you used and its date. Naming rules differ by provider and model generation. Name each artifact's owner and a reference that can't change, where one exists. A machine-readable format, such as CycloneDX ML-BOM or the SPDX 3.0 AI and Dataset profiles, lets tools check the manifest.

findings.title: Enforced gateway boundary
findings.requirement: Send MCP calls through a gateway or equivalent enforcement layer the agent cannot bypass. Choose controls for internal HTTP servers, public third-party services, and local stdio servers; private networking and mTLS are one internal deployment pattern, not universal MCP requirements. Authenticate each caller, preserve agent and delegated-subject identity, and authorize each action's tool, operation, resource, tenant, and arguments. Apply the same policy to direct calls, dynamic tools, CLI/code mode, and wrappers. Validate calls and responses, enforce rate limits, and log every decision. For HTTP OAuth, validate access tokens for the gateway's own audience, issuer, expiry, and scopes; obtain separately authorized backend credentials through a trusted issuer or supported exchange. Never accept a token for another resource or relay it unchanged as a substitute for backend authorization. Keep backend secrets and tokens away from agent-controlled execution paths. Restrict local process launch, files, environment, credentials, and network in the host or sandbox. Under MCP 2026-07-28, reject metadata-header/body mismatches before routing or policy relies on them. Isolate private caches by verified authorization context, tenant, resource, and policy version; share only data explicitly approved as public. Authorize explicit task/state handles on every operation; neither a connection nor self-reported metadata establishes identity. Where the gateway is an OAuth client, validate authorization-server issuer responses and protect discovery URLs against SSRF. Record protocol and extension versions and test each enabled extension's boundary, including task access/cancellation and MCP Apps sandbox, CSP, bridge messages, and UI-initiated tool authorization. Test bypass, cross-tenant access, malformed traffic, and required-check outages. Required checks fail closed.
